source: Atanasov, Witkowski, Ungar, Mellers, Tetlock (2020) Small steps to accuracy: incremental belief updaters are better forecasters (OBHDP 160:19-35)
finding: In the four-year IARPA tournament, the most accurate forecasters updated often and in small steps. Low-skill forecasters either confirmed old forecasts or made rare, large revisions. Three separate traits were tested: update frequency, update magnitude, confirmation rate.
numbers: About 400,000 forecasts, almost 500 geopolitical questions, four seasons. Core sample N=515 forecasters (10+ questions each). Mean 2.0 forecasts per question, mean absolute update 0.20 on the probability scale, 19% of forecasts were confirmations.
quote: Frequent, small revisions provided reliable and valid signals of skill.
limits: Observational. Volunteers, so effort is not controlled. Not advice to make small updates (see a05).
agent_relevance: S5 revise: the pattern to copy is many small evidence-driven revisions, not one big swing and not a blind restate.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) regression results
finding: Out-of-sample OLS on standardized Brier score: all three traits predicted accuracy. More updates, smaller updates, and fewer confirmations all went with better scores. Update magnitude was the strongest single behavioral predictor.
numbers: N=515, adj R2=0.28. Magnitude b=0.098 (t=8.69), confirmation b=0.028 (t=2.62, p=.009). With fluid intelligence in the model, magnitude b=0.105 (t=8.47); fluid IQ b=-0.064. Predicted raw Brier for an average untrained forecaster 0.36; frequency 1 SD above mean gives 0.33, 1 SD below 0.39; magnitude 0.10 gives 0.33, 0.31 gives 0.39; confirmation 1% gives 0.35, 37% gives 0.37; training gives 0.34.
limits: Standardized Brier scores. Effects are correlational except the training arm.
agent_relevance: Step size and update count matter as much as a training course. Log step size per revision as a metric.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) first vs last forecast split
finding: Small steps mark a good starting forecast. Frequent updating makes forecasts better over time. These are different routes to accuracy.
numbers: Magnitude vs initial-forecast accuracy: b=0.121 (t=10.94); vs last-forecast accuracy: b=0.044 (t=3.64). Frequency vs last-forecast accuracy: b=-0.181 (t=14.72); vs initial accuracy: b=0.008 (n.s.). Confirmation hurt both (initial b=0.030, final b=0.045). Magnitude link about null late in a question; frequency link stronger late.
limits: Small steps mostly reflect good priors, not a skill of stepping carefully.
agent_relevance: S5 gets accuracy from fresh evidence over time; a good early prior reduces how far S5 has to move.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) Brier decomposition by update style
finding: Small-and-frequent updaters had much lower calibration error and much higher discrimination than large-and-infrequent updaters.
numbers: Median splits (N: large-infrequent 164, small-frequent 164, large-frequent 93, small-infrequent 94). Raw Brier / calibration error / discrimination: large-infrequent 0.432/0.023/0.174; large-frequent 0.374/0.014/0.224; small-infrequent 0.394/0.010/0.200; small-frequent 0.292/0.002/0.293. Small-frequent about 0.5 SD better than average, large-infrequent 0.5 SD worse.
limits: Median-split groups; test questions differ from the classification questions.
agent_relevance: Both knobs count: the best style keeps resolution high and calibration error near zero.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) counterfactual step-size simulation
finding: Forcing smaller steps on everyone made scores worse. Making steps 20-30% larger helped only a tiny bit. Skilled forecasters were already near the best step size. So small steps are a sign of skill, not a trick to apply.
numbers: Simulated streams from 70% to 130% of actual step size. Smaller steps raised Brier by up to 4%. Larger steps cut Brier 0.3% on average. Small updaters would gain 0.7% from larger steps. 65% of forecasters would do better with larger steps, 25% with smaller, 10% with neither. Selecting small updaters gave a gain about 100x larger (Brier 0.22 vs 0.29, about 30% lower).
quote: Simply reducing update magnitude would have degraded accuracy.
limits: Slight net underreaction (Edwards-type conservatism). Excess volatility test of Augenblick and Rabin: only incremental updaters had appropriate volatility.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-cap step size. Size the move by evidence strength; a fixed damping factor is not supported.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) training mediation
finding: Randomized probability training made forecasters update in smaller steps, and that explained part of why training raised accuracy.
numbers: Roughly half randomly assigned to training each season. Untrained mean step 0.22 (SD 0.11) vs trained 0.19 (SD 0.09). Mediation: frequency 17% of training effect (CI -0.02 to 0.35), magnitude 29% (CI 0.09 to 0.55), confirmation under 1%. Training effect on accuracy about equal to +1.5 SD fluid intelligence.
limits: Training did not tell people to make small updates; it taught combining sources and base rates.
agent_relevance: Teach the cause (base rates, average several sources) and the small steps follow.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) personality, effort and boundary conditions
finding: Frequent updating tracked effort and open-mindedness (more logins, more news clicks, higher political knowledge and actively open-minded thinking). Small steps tracked fluid intelligence. Among top superforecasters the frequency-accuracy link was much weaker.
numbers: Test-retest r: frequency 0.98, magnitude 0.79, confirmation 0.83. Frequency vs magnitude r=-0.26; frequency vs confirmation r=0.51; magnitude vs confirmation r=0.02. Superforecaster sensitivity sample N=175; direction replicated.
quote: As average update frequency increases, the marginal benefit of additional revisions may be reduced or even reversed.
limits: Cue-learning work (Castellan 1973) says frequent updating can chase noise. Fildes et al. 2009 found small adjustments to model forecasts hurt.
agent_relevance: Whether to update and how much to update are separate decisions. Code should decide 'is this evidence new' and 'how big a move' separately.

source: Benjamin (2019) Errors in probabilistic reasoning and judgment biases, section 4 meta-analysis of bookbag-and-poker-chip updating
finding: Across incentivized and non-incentivized bookbag experiments, people underinfer: they move less than Bayes says. Underinference is by far the dominant direction. The first documented form was conservatism (Edwards, Phillips).
numbers: Meta-analysis of 16 papers (two-state binomial problems). Regression slope of subjective on Bayesian log-likelihood ratio c-hat=0.20 (SE 0.063) all studies; 0.38 (SE 0.028) incentivized only. Edwards urn example: 8 red 4 blue; correct posterior 97%, typical answer 70-80%.
quote: Underinference is by far the dominant direction of bias.
limits: Some overinference when signals are weak or the sample proportion equals a state rate; hypothetical-scenario studies (Kahneman and Tversky) emphasised other biases.
agent_relevance: Default model error on evidence is too little movement; push S5 to use the full likelihood ratio when the evidence is clean.

source: Benjamin (2019) stylized facts 2-6 (sample size and diagnosticity)
finding: Underinference grows with sample size and with how diagnostic each signal is. It is present after a single signal. Inference depends on the sample proportion, not on the count difference.
numbers: N=1 problems: mean c-hat=0.70 (SE 0.057) all, 0.86 (SE 0.078) incentivized. Every one of 9 papers that varied N found larger N gives smaller c-hat. Griffin and Tversky 1992 regression replicates in the meta-data.
limits: N=1 estimate rests on 16 problems.
agent_relevance: More evidence items does not mean proportionally more update; check S5 is not discounting a big batch.

source: Benjamin (2019) stylized facts 7-11 (priors and sequential samples)
finding: People also under-use prior odds (base-rate neglect, rarer than underinference). In sequential updating people do not pool signals; early signals and recent signals both weigh more than middle ones. One-third to one-half of subjects in some studies do not update at all after a signal.
numbers: Exponent on prior odds d-hat=0.60 (SE 0.066); sequential-sample d about 0.88 (SE 0.009). Primacy: Peterson and DuCharme 1967, Roby 1967, Dale 1968, De Swart and Tonkens 1977 (DuCharme 1970 found none). Recency: Pitz and Reinhold 1968, Shanteau 1970, Marks and Clarkson 1972, Grether 1992.
limits: Primacy and recency findings differ by task; not every study found both.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence matters; S5 should combine all evidence in code (log-odds sum) instead of letting the model weigh by position.

source: Benjamin (2019) on the conservatism model of Phillips and Edwards (1966)
finding: Phillips and Edwards (1966) wrote the conservatism model: posterior odds = (likelihood ratio)^c x prior odds with c under 1. Edwards (1968) argued for it with three points: stable c across sample compositions, underupdating even when subjects give their own likelihoods, and underinference at N=1.
numbers: c was known to be smaller when diagnosticity or sample size was larger (Phillips and Edwards 1966; Peterson, Schneider, Miller 1965).
limits: Alternatives: biased sampling-distribution beliefs, extreme-belief aversion, Bayes applied to noisy likelihood estimates; Benjamin says none is a clean win. Original 1966 and 1968 texts not opened (second-hand).
agent_relevance: Name the model: S5 as a damped log-odds update. Test whether the LLM shows c under 1.

source: Phillips and Edwards (1966) Conservatism in a simple probability inference task; Edwards (1968) Conservatism in human information processing
finding: Founding studies of conservatism: subjects revise posterior probabilities in the right direction but not far enough in poker-chip tasks. Known here only through Benjamin's review.
numbers: Edwards (1968) urn example: 70/30 red-blue urns, 8 red 4 blue draws; intuitive answer 70-80%, Bayes 97%.
limits: Original papers not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Historical anchor for the underreaction half of the S5 problem.

source: Mobius, Niederle, Niehaus, Rosenblat (2011) Managing self-confidence (NBER 17014)
finding: Subjects updated beliefs about their own IQ-quiz rank conservatively and asymmetrically (more for good news). The same task about a robot was closer to Bayes, so part of the bias is motivated, not only cognitive.
numbers: N=656 undergraduates. Four independent binary signals, each right with probability 75%. Subjects revised by only about 35% as much as Bayes. Positive-feedback subjects revised 15% more than negative-feedback ones. Two positive plus two negative signals (net zero information) still left subjects more confident. High-IQ and low-IQ subjects equally conservative. About 10% paid to avoid learning their type.
limits: Own-ability belief, a motivated domain; prior weight near 1.
agent_relevance: For an LLM forecaster the pull is toward its own earlier answer; make the update a function of evidence only (G2).

source: Mobius et al. (2011) robot placebo and the optimally biased Bayesian model
finding: Replacing own performance with a robot's performance reduced conservatism significantly and asymmetry somewhat, with the same signals and priors. Their model: a biased Bayesian who chooses how to read signal strength; conservatism arises as optimal bias.
numbers: Table 3 robot interaction terms around 0.33 and 0.24 (SE 0.05 and 0.04); exact cells read from a text extraction, check before quoting.
limits: Table values read from a text extraction.
agent_relevance: If the belief is 'mine', updating is damped. Show S5 the evidence with authorship hidden (G5).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd, Study 2 (LLM updates on crowd median)
finding: GPT-4 and Claude 2 gave a first forecast, then were shown the human crowd median and asked to update. Both improved. Update size tracked the gap. Updated forecasts still did worse than a plain average of model and human.
numbers: 31 binary Metaculus questions; 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts per model. GPT-4 Brier 0.17 (SD .13) to 0.14 (SD .11), p=.003. Claude 2 0.22 (SD .19) to 0.15 (SD .14), p<.001. Gains 17% to 28%. Gap vs update size r=0.88 (GPT-4), 0.87 (Claude 2). Intervals narrowed GPT-4 17.75 to 14.22, Claude 2 11.67 to 8.28 points. Versus simple average: GPT-4 0.13 (t(92)=2.58, p=.011), Claude 2 0.14 (t(92)=3.53, p=.001), average better.
quote: Updating itself is directionally correct but fails to improve upon a simple benchmark.
limits: Small question set; web-interface queries; evidence is one number (crowd median), so it is advice-taking as much as evidence integration.
agent_relevance: LLMs move toward new evidence in proportion to the gap but undershoot a simple average: an in-code weighted average may beat the model's own update.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 1 and prompt design
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs (median) matched a human crowd. Models show acquiescence (above 50%). The prompt told the model to start from base rates, then adjust to news, warning of over-adjusting and excess volatility.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD .12) vs 0.25 no-information, t(30)=-2.35, p=.026; vs human crowd 0.19 (SD .19), t(60)=0.19, p=.85. 925 human forecasters, 31 questions, 14 of 31 resolved yes, median model forecast 60%.
limits: Single three-month tournament; few questions; no ablation of the anchor-then-adjust sentence.
agent_relevance: The anchor-then-adjust prompt is the Tetlock recipe in text form; its effect alone is untested.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2503.17523 v3)
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs fail to update beliefs over rounds: accuracy plateaus after the first interaction. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian model's guesses (even its wrong early guesses) works better than fine-tuning on correct answers.
numbers: Flight-recommendation task, 5 rounds, 624 simulated users, accuracy tested on 100 held-out option sets per round. Bayesian Assistant final-round accuracy about 81%; random about 37%. Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro mostly flat after round 1. Humans (48 users) improved from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002) but stayed below Bayesian. Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time and beat oracle-tuned ones.
limits: Per-model bar values read from a figure text extraction; only the plateau and the 81% bound are firm.
agent_relevance: Without a scaffold, models stall; S5 needs explicit state (a belief table) kept by the program.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) generalization and failed remedies
finding: Chain-of-thought, numeric formats, 30 rounds and pretrained-only models did not fix updating. Bayesian-tuned models transferred to hotel recommendation, web shopping and human users, with a smaller gap for the real-world shopping task.
numbers: Fine-tune on 10 five-round interactions per user; full fine-tuning, DPO and LoRA gave similar results. With human users all models score well below the simulated-user level (near 80%) because human choices are inconsistent with stated preferences; for consistent humans the Bayesian LLM is much better than the original.
limits: Training-based fix; our project is training-free. Narrow, discrete hypothesis space. Larger models not tested.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought alone did not help updating here; supports G2 (code holds state) over asking the model to reason about update size.

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Ishii, He, Fung (2024) Belief revision: the adaptability of LLM reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: A logic-based revision test: does the model drop a conclusion when a new premise makes it unsafe, and keep it when the premise is irrelevant? Models trade one for the other.
numbers: 30 LMs tested; Belief-R built from ATOMIC, 1,912 total items (Belief Update and Belief Maintain subsets). Models over 6B parameters pass basic logic at 75% or more, but best BREU (mean of update and maintain accuracy) is at most about 50%. Llama-3 70B direct prompting: update 10.99%, maintain 92.09%, BREU 51.54%. Mixtral 8x22B: update 35.38%, maintain 36.57%. Chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve changed BREU by about 1%.
quote: LMs generally struggle to appropriately revise their beliefs in response to new information.
limits: Logical (Suppression Task) revision, not probabilistic. Table values read from a text extraction.
agent_relevance: LLM bias is toward keeping the old conclusion; use a signal-triggered re-derivation (G1/G2) when a new premise arrives.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency checks for language model forecasters (ICLR 2025)
finding: Logical-consistency checks across related questions (negation, conditional, expected evidence) track real Brier score. The ExpEvidence check is a belief-updating check: the forecast must equal the expected forecast after learning the evidence.
numbers: Correlation of consistency with Brier, scraped questions: Cond arbitrage 0.92 (frequentist 0.87), CondCond 0.78, Aggregated 0.62 (arbitrage) to 0.85 (frequentist). ExpEvidence arbitrage 0.20 (frequentist 0.77); on NewsAPI -0.11 and 0.06. o1-mini violates ExpEvidence on 47% (scraped) and 45% (NewsAPI) of tuples.
limits: Few forecasters tested; part of the correlation is that better models are both more consistent and more accurate. A flat 50% passes several checks.
agent_relevance: A code-checked martingale test (prior equals average of posteriors) is a cheap S5 guardrail that needs no ground truth.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: A retrieval-plus-reasoning system fed news to LMs and aggregated reasonings. It came close to the human crowd but did not pass it, except in selected settings.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Best base LM GPT-4-1106 0.208, random 0.250. Averaging system and crowd 0.146. Where the crowd is uncertain (0.3-0.7), 0.240 vs 0.247 (system slightly better). Fewer than 5 retrieved articles gave 0.238, near chance. System well calibrated without recalibration.
limits: Depends on retrieved article count. The paper does not isolate an update-size effect.
agent_relevance: New evidence helps only if enough is retrieved; S5 should hold its prior when evidence count is low.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: A dynamic benchmark of 1,000 questions; top LLM still behind superforecasters. LLMs given the crowd forecast on market questions did best.
numbers: Superforecasters (39 people) Brier 0.096 vs general public 0.121 and top LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (p<0.001); top LLM without crowd access 0.136.
limits: Leader changes as the benchmark updates; the 200-question human subset is a random sample.
agent_relevance: Models gain most when handed a strong prior to update from; the gap to superforecasters is the target.

source: Tetlock and Gardner (2015) Superforecasting; Tetlock and Boettger (1989) dilution effect; Mellers et al. (2015) drivers of prediction accuracy
finding: As cited in Atanasov et al.: Mellers 2015 found frequent updaters were more accurate; Tetlock and Gardner discuss incremental updating in superforecaster cases; Tetlock and Boettger found useful cues get diluted by non-diagnostic information. Not opened here.
numbers: No numbers taken here; see a01-a07.
limits: Second-hand citations only.
agent_relevance: Dilution is a risk for S5: filter non-diagnostic items before updating.

source: Augenblick and Rabin (2021) Belief movement, uncertainty reduction, and rational updating (QJE), as used in Atanasov 2020
finding: A test of over/under-reaction that needs no ground truth: compare the uncertainty a forecast stream resolves with how much it moved. Atanasov found tournament streams show excess volatility on average; only incremental updaters were appropriate.
numbers: Details in Atanasov appendix A5; original paper not opened.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: A ground-truth-free volatility test usable on agent forecast sequences.

source: Atanasov et al. (2020) discussion: two paradoxes and the Fildes et al. (2009) contrast
finding: Confirming a past forecast went with worse accuracy, so staying put is not a safe default. Whether to change and how much to change were unrelated choices, so the authors suggest a mixture model (chance of any update, then size). Experts adjusting statistical model forecasts did better with large changes, opposite to this study.
numbers: Confirmation vs magnitude r=0.02. Fildes et al. (2009): small adjustments to model forecasts made them worse, large ones improved them.
limits: Authors give two reasons for the divergence: forecasters updated their own earlier numbers, and competed purely on accuracy, whereas professionals may make small tweaks to signal effort.
agent_relevance: Model S5 as two code decisions: update-or-hold (triggered by a new check result) and move size (set by evidence weight). An agent that restates its answer after new evidence is the low-skill pattern.
